q: Which one is a gravity wall?
n: Figure A is a gravity wall, which resists earth pressure by its own mass. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering.

q: Which one is an anchored wall?
n: Figure E is held back by tieback anchors grouted into the soil behind: an anchored wall. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering.

q: Which one is a buttress wall?
n: Figure D has its ribs (buttresses) on the exposed front face: a buttress wall. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering.

q: Which one is a counterfort wall?
n: Figure C has its ribs (counterforts) buried in the backfill: a counterfort wall. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering.

q: Where is the ideal location for placing a shear wall?
n: Shear walls are best placed around elevator and stair cores, which are solid anyway and centrally located, limiting torsion. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 208; Arnold & Reitherman, Building Configuration and Seismic Design.

q: What is a shear wall mainly for?
n: A shear wall's main job is resisting lateral (wind and seismic) forces in its own plane. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 208.

q: What is the compressive strength of non-load-bearing concrete hollow blocks (CHB)?
n: Non-load-bearing CHB is commonly rated at about 350 psi compressive strength. Source: PNS 16 (concrete hollow blocks); Philippine manufacturer data.

q: What is the compressive strength of load-bearing concrete hollow blocks (CHB)?
n: Load-bearing CHB is commonly rated at about 700 psi compressive strength. Source: PNS 16; Philippine manufacturer data.

q: What is added inside hollow blocks to raise their load capacity?
n: Steel bars and grout in the cells turn hollow-block walls into reinforced masonry with higher load capacity. Source: NSCP 2015, Chapter 7 (masonry).

q: What is the minimum thickness of a load bearing CHB (Concrete Hollow Block) available in the Philippines?
n: Load-bearing CHB in the Philippines starts at 150 mm (6 in.) thick. Source: PNS 16; NSCP 2015 Chapter 7.

q: What horizontal member in a framed wall gives lateral support to the wall panels?
n: A girt is a horizontal member in a framed wall, spanning between columns to support the wall panels laterally. Source: MBMA; Ching.

q: What is the maximum spacing between stiffener columns in an ordinary CHB wall?
n: Stiffener (confining) columns in ordinary CHB walls are commonly spaced at about 3 m. Source: Philippine CHB construction practice; DPWH masonry guidelines.

q: A stiffener beam is required for a CHB wall if the wall height exceeds how many meters?
n: A stiffener (bond) beam is commonly required when a CHB wall exceeds about 3 m in height. Source: Philippine CHB construction practice; NSCP 2015 Chapter 7.

q: In CHB walls, at what spacing are horizontal reinforcing bars normally placed?
n: In Fajardo's CHB method, horizontal bars go every 3 layers (courses) of block. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB reinforcement tables).

q: What is the minimum size of reinforcing bars required for a 3-meter-high wall?
n: A 3 m CHB wall is commonly reinforced with at least 10 mm bars. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is the typical size of reinforcing bars used for an 8-inch concrete hollow block (CHB) wall?
n: 8-in. (200 mm) CHB walls typically take 12 mm bars. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; Philippine practice.

q: What is the minimum CHB thickness for non-load-bearing walls?
n: Non-load-bearing CHB walls are at least 100 mm (4 in.) thick. A 4-in. CHB is light and economical for interior partitions that carry no load. Source: PNS 16; Fajardo.

q: What is the minimum CHB thickness for load-bearing walls?
n: Load-bearing CHB walls need at least 150 mm. The thicker block gives enough bearing area and cell space for reinforcement and grout. Source: PNS 16; NSCP 2015 Chapter 7.

q: What wall holds back earth between different ground levels?
n: A retaining wall holds back earth between different ground levels. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is the most common type of failure in a retaining wall?
n: Retaining walls most commonly fail by overturning, from the moment of earth pressure about the toe (its moment arm). Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering.

q: What element at the base of a retaining wall adds stability?
n: The base slab (footing, with heel and toe) adds stability against overturning and sliding. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering.

q: What is provided through a retaining wall to relieve water pressure?
n: Weep holes through a retaining wall drain the backfill and relieve water pressure. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering; NSCP 2015 Sec. 304.

q: Which condition is most dangerous for a shear wall?
n: Many openings in a shear wall cut its stiffness and strength, the most dangerous condition. Source: Arnold & Reitherman, Building Configuration and Seismic Design.

q: Where do shear walls rest?
n: Shear walls must continue down to and rest on the foundation to deliver lateral loads to the ground. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 208 (load path).

q: For seismic reasons, where should the core walls go in a 15-storey building 15 m wide and 25 m long?
n: In a 15 × 25 m, 15-storey building, a central core keeps the centre of rigidity near the centre of mass and limits torsion. Source: Arnold & Reitherman, Building Configuration and Seismic Design; NSCP 2015 Sec. 208.

q: Which wall is designed to resist lateral forces in its own plane?
n: A shear wall is designed to resist lateral forces acting in its own plane. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 208 (definitions).

q: What boundary element of a diaphragm or shear wall resists axial stress?
n: A diaphragm chord is the boundary element of a diaphragm or shear wall that carries axial tension and compression. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 208 (definitions).

q: What is the nominal thickness of a concrete hollow block (CHB) for an exterior wall without plastering?
n: Unplastered exterior CHB walls are commonly 150 mm thick for durability and weather resistance. Source: Philippine CHB construction practice; Fajardo.

q: Which of the following is NOT a standard thickness for a CHB?
n: CHB comes in 4, 6 and 8 in. thicknesses. 10 in. is not standard. The standard block sizes (100, 150 and 200 mm thick) fit common wall and reinforcement details. Source: PNS 16; Fajardo.

q: Which of the following is NOT a commonly used CHB thickness?
n: Common CHB thicknesses are 4, 6 and 8 in. 5 in. is not common. Manufacturers produce only the standard 4, 6 and 8 in. thicknesses for walls. Source: PNS 16; Fajardo.

q: Brick masonry is weak in:
n: Brick masonry is weak in tension and strong mainly in compression. Source: NSCP 2015 Chapter 7; Ching.

q: How many CHB units are required for a wall measuring 10.2 meters in length and 3.3 meters in height, excluding a 300 mm lintel beam and 300 mm wide stiffener column? Include a 5% contingency allowance.
n: Net wall area = (10.2 − 0.3) × (3.3 − 0.3) = 29.7 m². At 12.5 CHB per m² that is 371.3 blocks, plus 5% = 389.8. The closest choice is 388. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (12.5 CHB/m²).

q: Horizontal bars used in CHB walls are typically installed at what spacing?
n: Horizontal CHB wall bars are typically every 3 layers, about 600 mm. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is the standard spacing for vertical reinforcement in a CHB wall?
n: Vertical bars in CHB walls are typically spaced 0.60 m. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What bar size is recommended for a 4-in. CHB wall?
n: A 4-in. CHB wall typically uses 10 mm bars. The cells of a 4-in. block are too small for larger bars, so 10 mm is used. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.
